#1 Let p:X→Yp:X\rightarrow Yp:X→Y be a covering and f:X→Zf:X \rightarrow Zf:X→Z be a map. What is the correct definition of the space of factorizations of fff through YYY up to homotopy ? I’d like a definition not as a space of maps Y→ZY \rightarrow ZY→Z that makes the diagram homotopy commutative, but rather something like a spaces of homotopies from fff to a map that factors on the nose.. It’s probably super elementary but for some reasons it gets me confused.

Basically this is the topological picture generalizing: given an inclusion of groups H⊂GH \subset GH⊂G and a morphism H→KH \rightarrow KH→K, classify the lifts G→KG\rightarrow KG→K along this map (either on the nose, or up to conjugation, depending of whether we’re taking (un)pointed spaces and maps).

Now suppose that the normal closure of HHH in GGG is the whole of GGG. Say, to simplify, there is another subgroup H′H'H′ of GGG which is conjugated to HHH and such that H,H′H,H'H,H′ generate GGG. Now assume I also have a morphism H′→KH' \rightarrow KH′→K (modulo details this is typically the sort of things I’d get from the topological picture, like if I have a morphism into KKK out of the fundamental groupoid of XXX with respect to the fiber over a chosen basepoint in YYY, e.g. if i know alll those points are sent to the same point in ZZZ). Now the question of whether these morphisms extends to a morphism from GGG becomes a condition, not extra structure (ie we have a surjective map from the free product H∗H′H*H'H∗H′ to GGG and a map from H∗H′H*H'H∗H′ to KKK so now the question is whether it factors through a quotient (rather than extends along an inclusion)). In particular if it does factors through it does so in a unique way.

What is the correct way to model this topologically, or groupoidally ? In what setting can I use that the normal closure of HHH is GGG to get some sort of unicity of factorization of some map ? I guess what I’m really asking is whether thee is a name for a functor F:C→DF:C\rightarrow DF:C→D such that End(d)\mathrm{End}(d)End(d) is generated by the images of the End(c)\mathrm{End}(c)End(c) for all ccc s.t. F(c)=dF(c)=dF(c)=d or something like that…

#2 Focusing on just the first paragraph (as I’d need to think more on what you say after “to simplify” :-)

The situation is this extension problem:

X→fZcov↓↗∃?Y \begin{matrix} X & \xrightarrow{f} & Z \\ {}^{\mathllap{\mathrm{cov}}} \big\downarrow & \nearrow_{ \mathrlap{\exists ?} } \\ Y \end{matrix} Xcov↓⏐​Y​f​↗∃?​​Z

I take it that the left map being a “covering” map is meant to say that it’s a principal bundle for some discrete group SSS? (Let me write SSS for “structure group”.)

In that case, the vertical map is the quotient by the action of SSS. In the 1-category of topological spaces this means that the extension exists and then uiquely, if and only if fff is equivariant, i.e. here: invariant, since the corresponding SSS action on ZZZ is taken to be trivial.

In the ∞\infty∞-category of spaces the analogous statement holds in the homotopy coherent sense.

What you are after, I gather, is a hands-on 1-category-theoretic model for this homotopy coherent situation.

The model category for this purpose is the Borel model structure (which works with spaces modeled as simplicial sets).

Using the Quillen equivalence here says that the derived mapping space space of homotopically SSS-equivariant maps fff is equivalently the derived mapping space of the slice sSet/W‾S\mathrm{sSet}_{/\overline{W}S}sSet/WS​ from Y→W‾SY \to \overline{W}SY→WS to Z×W‾→W‾Z \times \overline{W} \to \overline{W}Z×W→W (here W‾S\overline{W}SWS is the simplicial classifying space and Y→W‾SY \to \overline{W}SY→WS is the map that classifies the covering), and this is equivalently the derived mapping space in sSet\mathrm{sSet}sSet from YYY to ZZZ.

Now the SSS-action on XXX is free, by assumption of it being a covering space, which by this Prop means that XXX is cofibrant in the Borel model structure. Therefore the derived equivariant mapping space out of XXX is modeled by the mapping complex of naively SSS-invariant maps.

In conclusion, up to homotopy the maps fff that do extend to YYY are those which have a naively SSS-invariant representative, and these then extend uniquely.

I think.

That being said, even in the situation you describe there’s a small subtlety (I’m cutting hairs but it got me confused for a while). Namely it’s not quite true that fff factors uniquely, in the sense that I can have two maps s,t:Y→Zs,t:Y\rightarrow Zs,t:Y→Z which are not homotopic, but such that their precomposition with ppp are both homotopic to fff. Of course what you’re saying is still correct, but basically the set of solutions of the problem is, to me, the subspace of SSS-invariants functions which are homotopic to fff, I guess modulo SSS-equivariant homotopies.
